newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn makes move to force telecoms competition.
newsitem.headline: Bonn makes move to force telecoms competition.

text.p: The German government on Tuesday ordered phone giant Deutsche Telekom AG to grant rivals access to its local networks, a ruling that could prove crucial to ensuring competition in Europe's biggest telecoms market.

The ruling forces Deutsche Telekom to allow rivals to connect their networks directly to the telephone lines of businesses or residential customers without having to pay for any unwanted call switching services from Telekom.

By granting newcomers access to customers in the "last mile" of the telephone network, new companies hoping to compete against the incumbent monopoly will face lower costs and be able to price their services more competitively.

The ruling could finally break a deadlock in competition and it comes as government sources said Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet would appoint a post ministry official to head the new telecoms watchdog, the Regulatory Agency.

Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch, explaining the decision in an interview with Reuters, said the ruling was aimed at promoting competition and was visible evidence that Germany would exercise tough regulation.
"The last mile was always at the centre of the discussion," he said. "If the last mile cannot be bridged, or only with extraordinary costs, then competition will remain a theory."
"We have to prove that we are serious about regulation, otherwise companies with a dominant position in the market will press others up against the wall," he added.

Following complaints by rivals such as Mannesmann Arcor or the O.Tel.O. joint venture of utilities RWE AG and Veba AG , the ministry decided on May 28 that Telekom must offer rivals "unbundled interconnection".
But after Telekom failed to respond the ministry saw itself forced to issue a binding ruling and ordered Telekom to make such an offer by July 14 or face penalty proceedings.

Deutsche Telekom chairman Ron Sommer, speaking on the sidelines of a separate news conference in Bonn, compared such interconnection to "expropriation", but declined comment, saying he was not yet familiar with the ministry's decision.

"We want to consider this in peace and quiet and respond objectively," Sommer told reporters. Telekom later confirmed it had filed an appeal against the May 28 decision, which cannot stop the new ruling from taking effect but forms the basis of an appeal in Administrative Court that could overturn it.

As Europe prepares for full competition in telecoms from January 1, 1998, international alliances have formed to offer competitive services from corporate communications and long-distance calls to cable television and Internet access.
But the newcomers have patchy networks that do not reach into neighborhoods and city centres. Instead they still rent lines from Telekom in order to gain access to their customers.
The O.Tel.O consortium welcomed the government's ruling.
"The current confrontation with Telekom shows that we need a strong, competition-oriented regulator to open the telecommunications market," said O.Tel.O chairman Ulf Bohla.
Meanwhile, government sources said Kohl's coalition had agreed to appoint Dieter Scheuerle, a senior postal ministry official, to head the new telecoms Regulatory Agency.

Although widely expected, the choice has been controversial because of criticism from the telecommunications industry that Scheuerle could not be tough in regulating Deutsche Telekom, the incumbent monopoly which the government still controls.
The Regulatory Council, a body made of up representatives of state governments and parliament, had proposed appointing Peter Landsberg, former chairman of Alcatel SEL.
The new watchdog will be under the wing of the economics ministry and begins operating on January 1, 1998, when the telecoms sector is opened to full competition.

Scheuerle will head the new agency and have two deputies -- Arne Boernsen, the Social Democratic (SPD) chairman of parliament's postal affairs committee, and Volker Schlegel, head of the economics department at the German embassy in Washington.
Germany's Federation of Taxpayers called the decision a classic example of cronyism and sharply criticised Scheuerle's monthly salary of 18,535 marks as too high.
-- william.boston@reuters.com (Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150)
